# Medicine cabinet notes

What our pharmacist told us, written on the back of the receipt and typed up here.

## Acetaminophen

Adults can take 500 to 1,000 mg every 6 hours as needed, and no more than 3,000 mg in 24 hours. Read every label: many cold, flu and sleep products already contain acetaminophen, and the doses add up. Too much damages the liver, and alcohol makes that worse.

## Ibuprofen

Adults can take 200 to 400 mg every 6 to 8 hours with food, and no more than 1,200 mg a day without a doctor's advice. It is not for babies under 6 months. Skip it with kidney disease or stomach ulcers, late in pregnancy, or when dehydrated from vomiting.

## Aspirin

Aspirin is not for anyone under 19 with a fever or a virus, because of the risk of Reye syndrome. In adults it can irritate the stomach and thin the blood, so do not take it with other anti-inflammatory pills unless a doctor says so.

## Taking two medicines together

Acetaminophen and ibuprofen work differently, and a doctor may have you alternate them. The rule is never to take two products that share an active ingredient. Multi-symptom cold products often combine acetaminophen, a decongestant and a sedating antihistamine, so an allergy pill plus a nighttime cold medicine usually doubles up on antihistamine and makes you very drowsy. Check the "Drug Facts" label of each product and ask the pharmacist when in doubt.

## Giving medicine to children

Dose by weight, using the chart on the label, and measure with the syringe or cup that came in the box, never a kitchen spoon. Leave at least 4 hours between doses of acetaminophen and no more than 5 doses in 24 hours. Ibuprofen is not for babies under 6 months old; for them, acetaminophen is the choice after the doctor has seen the baby.

## Storing and throwing out medicine

Keep medicines in their original bottles, up high and locked if there are small children in the house. Toss anything past its expiry date or that smells or looks different. Drug take-back boxes are at the pharmacy.
